en: Preface to the Brief Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom Composed by the Tang Dynasty *Sāman* and Great Master Xianshou, Fazang.

Now, as for the primordial source and fundamental model, its profound stillness lies beyond all verbal devices; as for the subtle awakening and mysterious path, its deep and recondite nature transcends [all conceptualization].

Regarding these signs and images: although both the ultimate and the conventional are simultaneously extinguished, the two truths eternally persist; while both emptiness and existence have perished, the single flavor is constantly manifest.

This is because true emptiness has never failed to exist—it is through existence that emptiness is discerned; and illusory existence has never begun to be non-existent—it is through emptiness that existence is clarified.
Because there is existence within emptiness, it is not existent; because there is emptiness within existence, it is not empty. This non-emptiness...

Emptiness. It is empty yet not annihilated; it is the existence of non-existence, and existence that is not permanent. Once the four attachments have perished, the hundred negations are simultaneously dispelled.
This is what is meant by the profound purport of Prajñā. If one were to detail its applications exhaustively, the words would exceed two hundred thousand stanzas.
If one grasps its essential pivot, the principle is exhausted within these fourteen lines. Thus we know that the teaching which elucidates the Truth may expand or contract according to circumstances;
yet the宗 (zong), which transcends words, is perfectly pervasive by nature and reveals itself in all things.

This *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* is truly what I call a lofty torch illuminating the dark thoroughfare and a swift vessel for crossing the sea of suffering. In rescuing beings and guiding the deluded, nothing surpasses this.
Thus, Prajñā takes spiritual discernment as its essence, while Pāramitā takes reaching the other shore as its function.

The *Hṛdaya* (Heart) reveals the essential and subtle point of return, whereas the *Sūtra* threads together the verbal teachings. Following the Dharma through metaphors, it takes the elucidation of the ultimate meaning as its title;
hence it is called the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.

This preface is concise yet rich in meaning; its phrasing is free from superfluous branches. Contemplating its "empty truth," one finds that it never fails to exist, and by means of existence itself, it distinguishes emptiness (and so forth).
These twelve turns of phrase strip away everything to reveal a single, intimate, and rigorous reality of empty truth.
Were it not for one who possesses both eyes, none could speak thus. Whenever I recite these words, I am filled with a sense of clarity and inspiration.

Regarding the *sū*, *roma*, and *asthi* [relics], many have obtained their seals and certificates. It is truly impossible to conceal the Master’s excellence, nor would I dare to keep it private within my own mind.
I respectfully record this at the beginning of the volume to share it with the world, so that those of like mind in the future may behold its splendor.
Preface to the Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom.
The Heart Sūtra spoken by the Buddha consists of fifty-three words from beginning to end, yet it is able to clarify the wondrous meaning within the twelve divisions of the Great Canon;

no other sūtra can compare to it. Therefore, it is called the *Nītārtha* (Definitive Meaning) Heart Sūtra. As for why the sūtra is called "Heart" (*hṛdaya*): [it is because it contains the essential core of all teachings].
The mind is that which presides over the single body and operates through its hundred limbs.
How great indeed is the significance of the mind! Yet, among later commentators, none have shed light upon the meaning of the sūtra text.

It is only the *Heart Sūtra* Brief Commentary (*Lüeshù*) by the Tang dynasty eminent monk Xianshou, whose name was Fazang, and [the work] by Zhenjue, whose name was Wencai, [that provide such illumination].
The *Zhuhuidengji* (Collection of Lamp-like Commentaries on Wisdom) exhaustively abridges the details of the sub-commentaries. These two commentaries do not deviate from the original text;

their principles are substantial and practical, though the language is plain and the meaning pure. However, the structural divisions (*ketiao*) are so numerous and minute that for a beginner, the spirit may wander and the breath falter;
viewing them all at once, there is no point of entry. Furthermore, as for Mr. Song Qianxi of the Xuankui Academy, he followed the Xianshou school of Zongle.
The commentaries of various masters such as Gushan and Guyu, though their interpretations clarify the meaning, are not without omissions and oversights.
Alas! It is evident that this sutra cannot be annotated in a perfunctory manner, and the task of providing a commentary is truly difficult.
Furthermore, among the three baskets of the Buddha’s teachings—the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—all that are designated as Sūtra or Vinaya are...
Proclaimed from the golden mouth of the World-Honored One, it entered the ears of the Venerable Ānanda without a single word being altered from beginning to end.
When the Buddha reached the Twin Śāla Trees, he commanded Ānanda to compile and collect into sūtras all the teachings he had expounded during the forty-nine years [of his ministry].

At the beginning of all sutras, the four characters "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam) must invariably be employed; this is intended to demonstrate the principle of recording rather than composing.

Furthermore, during the Buddha’s lifetime, among the bodhisattvas present in the assembly—such as Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta—who were the leaders of immeasurable bodhisattvas from the ten directions, none of them were ever seen preaching the Dharma. Even if they had spoken, [it was not recorded].
These are not the words of the Buddha; how would Ānanda dare to collect and include them in the Tripiṭaka? Is it possible to mix water with milk?
From this, one may know that there is no doubt the Heart Sūtra was spoken by the World-Honored One.

Otherwise, why would the *Lüeshu* (Brief Commentary) state that although this sūtra of fourteen lines is concise in its phrasing, its meaning is complete in every respect, and it is capable of encompassing the six hundred fascicles [of the Prajñāpāramitā]?
This essential mystery is, in fact, the *dhāraṇī* that encompasses all the sūtras.

In this brief commentary, the section from "Avalokiteśvara" to "crosses over all suffering and distress" is designated as the "Section on Briefly Indicating the Essential Framework," while the section beginning with "Śāriputra" is designated as the "Section on Extensively Expounding the Actual Meaning.
By examining the text in detail according to these headings and outlines, one will finally understand the structural脉络 (pulses/lineaments) of the Heart Sūtra.
This is precisely what is meant by "opening the dense ignorance of ten thousand ages. For the purport of the Heart Sūtra lies in Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddhas of the three periods rely upon it and immediately attain Bodhi; the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages rely upon it and immediately realize Nirvāṇa.
One who clearly understands Prajñā-pāramitā finds that the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths and so forth are all unworthy of recollection. Thus it is said:
"Studying the Dharma for a thousand days is not equal to studying Prajñā for a single day. How could those who seek transcendence of the world bypass Prajñā to long for other teachings?

With my shallow views and meager understanding, how would I dare to take pleasure in eccentricity or engage in contentious debate with venerable elders? Nor would I dare to venture upon a presumptuous commentary.
Explanation: Coming as a latecomer in my ignorance, I have based this exposition solely on the commentaries of the two masters Wén and Tài (Wéncai).
At intervals, I have ventured to append my own views to supplement their omissions; this is merely the foolishness of one who has gained a single insight.
It is my hope that beginners among students will not be like "dwarfs watching a performance," and that this work may perhaps provide some small benefit.
Written in the spring of the Dinghai year of the Wanli era by Xie Guangguang of Yanhuhei, Fujian,
at the depths of Ziyang Dongtian in Qiantang,
as an Exegesis on the Meaning of the Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom (*Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*).
Compiled by the Daoist Hei-hu Xie Zi of Min-Jian Yi-li, Guang-guang;
and the monk Liao-huan of Wu-ling, formerly a Jinshi (Metropolitan Graduate), Hu Xiao.
[The Buddha taught that among all men and women in the world, regardless of noble or humble status, if one is willing for even a single thought-moment...]

When one contemplates the mind, then that person’s own nature is already present. There is no need for deliberation or contrivance. Why? Because when the self-nature is fully realized, it serves as the master in responding to phenomena; thus, affairs cannot disturb it. How peaceful and joyful this is! This dharma-gate of "contemplation" (guan) is the pivot of the myriad practices (*sādhana*).

Qingliang said: "The myriad practices are condensed into the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*); the six perfections are subsumed within the three trainings—precept, concentration, and wisdom. The three trainings are subsumed within cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Cessation and contemplation are rooted in the single mind. Cessation is the initial gateway for subduing the fetters;

contemplation is the essential method for severing delusions. If one cultivates cessation and contemplation, all matters are completed. If a person does not contemplate for even a single thought-moment, the mind has already been deluded by external objects. Once the mind is submerged in objects, all afflictions will arrive in succession. Thus, one attains autonomy.

How could such joy be obtained? Now, those who study contemplation should not contemplate with their eyes; they should contemplate with their minds. When the mind contemplates its own substance, it immediately attains mastery. When one forgets the substance and contemplates external objects, afflictions arise. Since everything encountered by the eye is an object, who could fail to contemplate it?

If one contemplates without contradicting the essence, its function is immediately numinous and wondrous. Contemplating the mind in this way establishes the path to Buddhahood. As the Sūtra says: "The equal and true Dharma-realm cannot be reached by non-practice;

if one can intermittently contemplate the mind, one can both practice and reach it. Regarding the brief commentary that takes "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" as a phrase, this refers to the person who contemplates the mind; it does not mean there is actually a single bodhisattva who bears that name.

I maintain that the single phrase "Avalokiteśvara" is the fundamental principle for studying the Buddha, while "practicing profound Prajñā" is the fundamental principle for cultivating a bodhisattva. Those who now wish to cultivate...

The path of the Bodhisattva is somewhat complex in its methods; it requires that one first practice the profound Prajñā-wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) and attain the *pāramitās*.

Only when reaching the shore of tranquil and pure *nirvāṇa* can one then clearly perceive that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)—which arise based on human nature—are originally devoid of substantiality.

Once *nirvāṇa* is realized, those aggregates, through this insight, all return to emptiness and conventionality, leaving only *nirvāṇa* manifest. This is because one first realizes *nirvāṇa* and subsequently destroys the five aggregates; only then does this occur.

He delivers [all beings] from the hardships and calamities of all obstructions, terrors, inverted views, and delusive dreams. (It is not that he first delivers them from these hardships; therefore, the *Lüshù* states briefly: "When one realizes and perceives true emptiness, suffering and affliction are thereby exhausted.")

One first distances oneself from the two kinds of birth and death: the *pariccheda* (segmented) and the *pariṇāma* (transformative). Yet those who study today, at the very outset, become mired in [formalism], closing their eyes and sitting in stillness to sweep away deluded thoughts, hoping that once delusions are exhausted, they will perceive the true nature (*dharmatā*).

Practitioners who act in this way greatly contravene the intent of the Buddha. How can they know that delusions are as numerous as dust motes? With the cognitive views of ordinary beings, how could one ever achieve liberation? I maintain that to eliminate delusive dust, one must realize *nirvāṇa*;

to realize *nirvāṇa*, one must practice *prajñā*. If *prajñā* is not practiced, then *nirvāṇa* is not realized; if *nirvāṇa* is not realized, then suffering and calamity cannot be eliminated. Therefore, the *Heart Sūtra* takes *prajñā* as its core principle. These two preceding sections are briefly annotated and titled "The Section Briefly Marking the Essential Outlines," which constitutes the two main pillars of learning the Buddha and learning the Bodhisattva.

This is the introduction. The subsequent section, which extensively sets forth the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*), consists of eight items within that teaching. The principles of the Heart Sūtra transcend all meditative absorptions and disciplines; they are pure, subtle, and refined, such that none but those of superior intelligence can comprehend them.

Among the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, Śāriputra was one of such superior intelligence. At that time, as the Buddha was about to extensively set forth these items, he specifically addressed his disciple foremost in wisdom, Śāriputra, saying:
"Now, form (*rūpa*) is not different from emptiness (*śūnyatā*); emptiness is also not different from form. (This first section is briefly annotated.)

This is called the "unimpeded contemplation of emptiness and conventionality. The Buddha further said: "Form (*rūpa*) is itself emptiness" (this section is the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional). "Emptiness is itself form" (this section is the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness).

Regarding the remaining four aggregates (*skandhas*), the Buddha, for the sake of brevity, summarizes them by saying: "Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these four aggregates are also like this. (The four turns of phrase regarding the aggregate of form are applied identically to the others;

this section is developed based on the preceding text concerning the emptiness of the five aggregates and the method of the term "contemplation" [*vipaśyanā*]. The *Lüshù* states: "Contemplate form as emptiness to accomplish the practice of cessation (*śamatha*); contemplate emptiness as form to accomplish [the practice of insight]. )

In the practice of contemplation, emptiness and form are non-dual; only when cessation and contemplation proceed together does one reach the ultimate. Now, regarding the two terms "form" and "emptiness," students must clarify them for themselves; by no means should you merely parrot them at the sound of others' voices. This emptiness, which is not different from form, is not a state of nothingness.

Rather, it is the name for the true nature that truly exists within every person. As for "form," it does not refer solely to what is seen by the eye; sound, fragrance, touch, and mental phenomena are all form. It is the name for all external objects and things.

What is called "not different" and further described as "identical" expresses the intent to teach people to harmonize with the light and blend with the dust, merging form and dissolving into emptiness. One must strictly avoid shunning clamor and pursuing stillness; this is the sickness of those who seek to eliminate delusive thoughts and grasp a "true nature" through medical treatment. If a student...

Awaken to prajñā. By employing prajñā in engagement with phenomena, even phenomena themselves become prajñā. If one clearly realizes that phenomena are prajñā, then responding to things will likewise be without delusion. Huìdēng said: "Phenomena are empty while principle is real; to respond to the empty with the real is like water subduing waves."

The characteristics of the waves naturally exhaust themselves. One who understands this Dharma need not move a step to swiftly realize Bodhi. However, this Tathāgatagarbha—the emptiness of the oneness of mind and object—is difficult for those with heavy afflictions and meager merit to encounter.
Out of compassion for us, the Buddha, seeing that we did not realize the pearl within our own clothing, again called to Śāriputra to describe this true-mark Tathāgatagarbha.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "When these dharmas of the five aggregates are emptied, at that very moment, the state of emptiness must necessarily manifest."

When these characteristics (marks) emerge, one then accords with the principle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Otherwise, one falls into the void of the emptiness of dharmas. These marks are neither empty nor existent; they are extremely difficult to describe.

In the following passage, the Buddha presents the two poles of "non-arising and non-ceasing" to realize the marvelous treasure of the middle way. I say that this section is the direct pointing to the gate of the true mark (*dharmatā*). To briefly explain "non-arising and non-ceasing" according to their stages: it refers to the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) prior to the Path.

Because ordinary beings die here and are born there, transmigrating through long kalpas, this is the stage of arising and ceasing. True emptiness is free from this, and thus it is called non-arising and non-ceasing. Now, explaining according to their nature: when the Śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle are deluded, they pursue external objects and give rise to false thoughts, which constitutes...

When one awakens, detachment from objects and the cessation of delusion constitute extinction. Because one has not yet realized the mark of emptiness, non-arising is itself extinction, and non-extinction is itself arising; movement and stillness are merely these two extremes of busyness. If one possesses the true mark of ultimate emptiness, then when responding to objects and moving, [the mind remains unmoved].

To see through objects as being external conditions and false is not to follow after them; this is merely indicated by their having the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Although it is said that thoughts arise, in reality, even arising is non-arising.

One should understand that when mental deliberations are still, they appear to be in a state of extinction (*nirvāṇa*); yet within that extinction there is the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and thus extinction is also non-extinction. (Briefly explaining "neither stained nor pure" according to the stages:

although the stains of obstruction and defilement have not yet been entirely eliminated in the stages of Bodhisattvas and others on the Path, their practice of purity has already been cultivated; this is called the stage of "stained-purity. True Emptiness transcends this, hence it is said to be "neither stained nor pure. Now, explaining according to the nature, within the stage of the Pratyekabuddha...

Those who ride upon the vehicle [of the teachings] weary of clamor and seek tranquility; thus, their knowledge and vision possess both defilement and purity. However, for one who has realized the mark of emptiness, even when responding to phenomena and dwelling amidst the dust of the world, no defilement is seen;
and even when realizing that the nature of the mind is serene and still, no purity is seen. (This brief outline explains "neither increasing nor decreasing" by way of the stages:

within the stage of the Buddha’s fruition after the Path, the afflictions and hindrances of birth and death—which were not exhausted in the past—are now exhausted; this is "decrease. The myriad virtues produced through cultivation—which were not perfected in the past—are now perfected; this is "increase. True emptiness is free from these, and is therefore called "neither increasing nor decreasing. This refers to the nature itself.

Commentary: This refers to those of the Supreme Vehicle (Mahāyāna). When they awaken, clarity arises, as if there were an increase; when they are deluded, clarity is lost, as if there were a decrease. However, for one who realizes the true mark of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā-tathatā*), because this true mark does not exist by virtue of being produced by a sage, when they abide in the stage of a sage, they do not see it as having any increase.

Since its nature and marks are originally and fully possessed, even when they abide in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they do not see it as having any deficiency. Indeed, one who realizes the mark of the true mark does not fall into nihilistic emptiness, nor...

To be obstructed by existence is called the "pure and wondrous form-body. The Buddha said: "This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. Who is able to believe, awaken to, and tread upon this form of the true mark of empty reality?

When the five aggregates are not illuminated, they are naturally empty; when the six sense organs are not cleansed, they are naturally pure; when the six sense objects are not swept away, they are naturally clear; when the six consciousnesses do not revolve, they are naturally wisdom. The immeasurable Dharma gates are all manifestations of this true mark of empty reality, subsumed within this single Dharma.

Therefore, within this true mark of empty reality, there is no obstruction of the aggregate of form, nor is there any obstruction of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Possessing this true mark—
This is the Dharma; thus, no other dharmas are employed. Therefore it is said: there is also no washing away of the dharmas of the six faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;

there is also no sweeping away of the dharmas of the six objects—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*); and there is also no turning of the minor dharma of the eye-element within the eighteen elements, up to and including the non-turning of the eighteen elements such as the consciousness-element.

(The *Lüshù* briefly designates this section as the "Gate of the Opening and Closing of Dharmic Characteristics. Indeed, within the Gate of the Characteristic of Emptiness, not only are these enumerated dharmas absent, but furthermore...)

There is also no exhaustion of ignorance (within the twelve links of dependent origination). Why is this? For ignorance, once awakened to, is itself true emptiness; true emptiness, once deluded, again becomes ignorance.

Since ignorance arises from delusion and ceases through awakening, although it has no fixed substance, if the mind is deluded even once, ignorance immediately manifests. Thus, one cannot say that it is utterly exhausted and non-existent. Therefore it is said: "There is also no exhaustion of ignorance.

(For this empty characteristic of ignorance is fundamentally not two separate things. Yongjia said: "The actual nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory, transformed, empty body is itself the Dharma-body. These words are most profound.)

One perceives that there is flavor. Suffering and calamity arise from ignorance; therefore, ignorance is the primary evil among the twelve links of dependent origination. Now, having realized the mark of emptiness, since ignorance is already absent, its remaining cohorts—dependent on volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), dependent on consciousness (*vijñāna*), dependent on name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), dependent on the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), dependent on contact (*sparśa*), dependent on feeling (*vedanā*), dependent on craving (*tṛṣṇā*), dependent on grasping (*upādāna*), and dependent on becoming (*bhava*)—are likewise all absent.
It does not stop at merely being without these. It extends even to "no" (all) aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

(Since a person possesses a body, they must inevitably undergo aging and death; yet here it is said they do not exist. The Buddha speaks in terms of the fundamental nature: because the true nature of a person is indestructible throughout ten thousand kalpas, it is without death and without birth.)

Therefore it is said: "There is no old age and death. Although in their fundamental nature there is no old age and death, the physical body cannot avoid them; how could one say they are utterly extinguished? Therefore it is said: "Nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.

(This section is briefly titled in the commentary as the "Gate of the Direct and Reverse Order of Dependent Origination. Not only do the aforementioned dharmas not equal the effortless [simplicity] of the true mark (*dharmatā*), but even regarding the Dharma of the Four Truths—though they constitute the Dharma-treasure of the Mahāyāna—the True Emptiness can likewise encompass them.
Therefore it is said: "Within the gate of the true mark, it is also...")

There is no suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path [the Four Noble Truths]. This section is briefly titled by the *Lüshu* (Brief Commentary) as the "Gate of Defiled and Pure Cause and Effect. A detailed explanation is found in the "Resolution of Doubts.

The subsequent section, "Neither wisdom nor attainment," is briefly titled by the *Lüshu* as the "Gate of Object and Subject, Wisdom and Capacity. The external object is the "object" (*suo*); internal wisdom is the "subject" (*neng*). The student, through the internal capacity of prajñā-wisdom, perceives the principle of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Having attained this principle, one first becomes free from the various phenomena of the aforementioned external objects. Now that these objective phenomena no longer exist, yet the wisdom and principle still remain without having departed—this section is extremely difficult to describe. Therefore, a metaphor is provided: the principle of true perception is likened to a medical prescription, while the disturbances of all phenomena are likened to... [the illness].

Regarding illness: the wisdom of *prajñā* is likened to medicinal herbs. Once the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is realized, what further use is there for *prajñā*? It is like a disease that has been cured; one need not apply medicine again. To take medicine when one is already free of illness is to fear that the medicine itself will give rise to another ailment.

Now that the phenomena are empty, *prajñā* must also be exhausted—that is, the [conceptual] wisdom is absent. Although *prajñā* is exhausted, the principle of seeing reality as it is still remains, just as the prescription remains even after the medicine has been taken. If one were now to discard the very prescription one had obtained, then both would be gone altogether. This is just like peeling a plantain tree:
once you have peeled it down until there is nowhere left to grasp, only the wondrous treasure revealed is that which is neither illness, nor medicine, nor prescription. Therefore, it is said:

"There is neither ignorance nor attainment. (The student studies until they reach this field of non-attainment. It is profound, silent, solitary, and precarious; practitioners have vanished from its tracks. Truly, there is no place to ask for guidance.

One must personally rouse one's spirit and open one’s eyes to establish a firm resolve. Otherwise, one will fall into that deep pit of delusion, from which one will not emerge for ten thousand kalpas. Do not resent me for not having explained it all today. To escape the suffering of birth and death, one must pass along this path; there is no way to evade it.

The subsequent passage, "Because there is nothing to be attained," is a sentence that restates what precedes and introduces what follows. The *Lüeshu* (Brief Commentary) states: "Because" (*yi*) means "by means of"; "therefore" (*gu*) means "the reason why. This refers to the study of the realization of birth and death.

This is because, by taking "non-attainment" as the cause (as mentioned previously), one is subsequently able to attain the fruits of *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*. These two fruits are attained by "attaining through non-attainment. If a practitioner harbors even the slightest thought of attainment, they will be obstructed by it, and these two fruits cannot be attained.

This sutra concludes the Dharma with these three characters, "non-attainment"—is this not its singular purpose? It is precisely where the Elder Gautama’s heart was most earnest. Guifeng said: "Prajñā..."
If one takes non-attainment as the skillful means, and Perfect Enlightenment takes the departure from signs as the skillful means,
this is it. Now, when a Bodhisattva enters the stage of non-attainment by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, within his mind there is for the first time no [attachment to] any fame,
profit, desire, joy, anger, love, or hatred.

Obstruction. Because there are no obstructions, one is free from the fearful dread of gain and loss. When the Bodhisattva’s practice reaches this point, delusions do not obstruct the mind and objects do not obstruct wisdom;

externally, there is no fear of demons or enemies, which means adverse conditions have ceased. From this, one is finally able to distance oneself from the deluded, intoxicated dreams of sound and form.
Reaching this stage, there are no internal inversions caused by the obstacles of delusion, meaning evil causes are exhausted. Within this interval, for the first time—
Ultimate [Nirvana] (the fruit of cessation, the sovereign perfection of quiescence, wherein the Bodhisattvas have fully realized deathlessness and birthlessness).

All Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time (who have entered the ground of non-attainment) likewise do so by relying on the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Therefore, as soon as they realize *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (the fruit of wisdom, the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment), [they attain it].

(Commentary by Layman Longshu: In Sanskrit, *an* means "non-" or "without"; *uttara* means "above" or "supreme"; *sam* means "perfectly"; *yak* means "rightly"; *saṃ* means "equally"; and *bodhi* means "enlightenment.")

"Ya" means equality. "Miao" means equality. "Bodhi" means awakening. To explain it in detail: it is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (Unsurpassed Perfect Complete Awakening). To explain it briefly: it is simply called "awakening. Because the true nature of every person has nothing that can surpass it, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).

Furthermore, from the Buddhas of the ten directions above down to the most minute insects and sentient beings below, this nature is perfectly equal in its characteristics; thus it is called "perfectly equal" (*samyak*). This awakened nature is perfectly luminous and universally illuminating; it neither departs nor arrives, pervading the great chiliocosms while entering the smallest pore.

Thus it is called "perfect awakening" (*saṃbodhi*). One who attains the fruit of this perfect awakening is therefore a Buddha. While remaining within these three realms, one is detached from them and shall no longer undergo the cycle of rebirth.

(The above text is a clear manifestation of profound principles. It enables those who follow the text to understand its meaning and practice according to the Dharma. For those who possess sincere faith and diligent practice, the net of Māra will naturally tear asunder, the five aggregates will suddenly become empty, and the afflictions of the six sense organs will gradually subside until suffering and calamity are silently eliminated.
Thus, the fruit of Buddhahood will certainly be realized.)

The following spells that are explained hereafter are called the "Secret Prajñā. "Secret" means esoteric; it signifies that they cannot be fully explicated, but rather that one should simply maintain faith and recite them. Thus, calamities and karmic obstacles will naturally be eliminated, while merit and wisdom will increase.

There is a subtle assistance that aids the practitioner’s progress on the Path. If one is dull-witted due to greed, anger, and ignorance, and if the deep-seated habitual tendencies of past karma have not yet been removed, there is absolutely no possibility of escaping their shackles without relying on the power of these divine spells.
In the subsequent passage, the Buddha first praises the supreme excellence of the Secret Prajñā spell’s power, saying:
Therefore, know that this *prajñāpāramitā* is a divine mantra. It is not like ordinary mantras;
it is a mantra of great power that resolves the karmic enmities of past lives. It is a great illuminating mantra that clears away all the ignorance and dullness of the human mind.

Among all the mantras found in the various sūtras, there is not a single one more sublime or excellent than this mantra. Therefore, it is said: "There is no mantra superior to this. There is no [mantra] equal to this *prajñā* mantra.
This [mantra] is a general mantra that can eliminate all sufferings, calamities, obstacles, and afflictions of sentient beings within the three realms.

These words of praise for this mantra, which are most excellent and sublime, are all true words; they are not false or deceptive speech. Having praised this mantra, the World-Honored One then spoke this mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā.
He spoke the mantra as follows: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate*.
*Āraṇyaketi bodhi svāhā.* This silent recitation of the Heart Sūtra, as explained by Meilao, is direct in principle and coherent in meaning; it is extremely beneficial for beginners.

Through this, one first attains access to the original text of two hundred and sixty characters, which uniquely elucidates Prajñāpāramitā. It is truly the correct path for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to realize the fruit of enlightenment.
Even Pratyekabuddhas, Pratyayabuddhas, and Śrāvakas have not yet understood its essential core;

how then could ordinary beings, icchantikas, or followers of external paths believe in its spiritual power? Furthermore, it is neither remote nor abstruse, manifesting both secretly and openly within the space of a single thought-moment of a person.
If one is truly able to practice both simultaneously without contradiction, who else could they be but a son born from the Buddha’s own mouth?
This concludes the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom* by the monk Liaohan.
